transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Start time: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Head of ML - Mercantile), Jordan Blake (Infra Lead), Priya Singh (CISO)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro — I'm Alex, AE at Redwood, and Samir is our solutions engineer, he'll cover the technical bits. Maya, Jordan, Priya, thanks for joining.
[00:12] Maya: yeah thanks, uh quick context: we're evaluating options for moving our customer-facing LLM features off the hosted proof-of-concept and onto something production grade. primary asks: data isolation, deterministic latency, and cost predictability.
[00:28] Alex: perfect. is the team leaning dedicated or private, or still open?
[00:32] Maya: leaning dedicated — reserved GPUs in our cloud account or Redwood-managed dedicated pools? we want isolation but not full on-prem — so dedicated sounds right.
[00:40] Jordan: to add, we need VPC peering and we need control of keys — KM S access isn't negotiable. also curious about burst — we have unpredictable spikes during statement cycles.
[00:52] Samir: ok, good. we routinely do dedicated where we provision reserved GPU pools with VPC connectivity and KMS integration. solitary note: "KM S" in transcript sometimes mis-typed — we do mean KMS HSM integrations, yes.
[01:05] Priya: SOC2 plus some regional data residency constraints. we might need audit logs retained longer than default. can you support that?
[01:12] Alex: yes, enterprise add-ons include longer log retention and custom SLA. we'll share the security pack.
[01:17] Samir: on the capacity question: typically customers pick a baseline reserved capacity (for predictable throughput) and configure burst capacity that either comes from a shared Redwood pool or from transient reserved instances — we can map that to your throughput profile.
[01:30] Jordan: can you explain how burst works — what if our qps doubles for 10 minutes — will requests queue, degrade, or route to hosted models?
[01:40] Samir: great q. we support policies: 1) scale up reserved pool with autoscaler (time to spin up depends on instance availability), 2) burst to Redwood shared capacity (same API, but routed off the dedicated pool) with fallback to a smaller model variant, or 3) queue at the edge with graceful degradation.
[01:54] Maya: fallback to smaller variants worries product — quality regression. how do you measure quality vs cost tradeoffs?
[02:02] Samir: we provide model variant recommendations and quantization profiles per workload. for critical routes you can pin a model version; for non-critical you can allow fallback. we also provide evaluations (prompt sets) so you can see regression risk before enabling fallback.
[02:18] Jordan: time to scale — if we rely on autoscaling, what's the typical latency hit during scale up?
[02:24] Samir: cold start for a new GPU node is often a few minutes; we mitigate via continuous warm pools, fast startup images, and kernel preloads. for p95-sensitive endpoints we recommend reserving headroom (e.g., 20-30%). alternatively we use burst to shared capacity which is quicker but may not offer the same isolation.
[02:42] Priya: what about encryption in transit and at rest? do you integrate with our KMS or does Redwood hold keys?
[02:49] Alex: we support customer-managed keys in both Dedicated and Private. in Dedicated we can integrate with your cloud KMS or bring-your-own-HSM. logs and KV cache encryption supported.
[02:59] Maya: curious about cost model — reserved capacity commit vs pay-as-you-go hosted. need a clear example with numbers for our traffic profile.
[03:07] Alex: we'll send a pricing spreadsheet. rough example: a 4-GPU reserved pool for steady throughput plus burst credit costs X vs hosted per-token at Y; Samir will build a benchmark using your sample workload to get concrete numbers.
[03:20] Jordan: concurrency numbers — our expected steady qps is ~120 QPS across 5 routes, peak up to 400 QPS for short windows. average token lengths 90-120. does that sound feasible?
[03:33] Samir: yes that's in a typical range. we need more detail on request distribution and sequence length variance. we'll use that to size batching, KV cache hit expectations, and GPU memory (kv cache impacts).
[03:46] Maya: also multi-tenant considerations — we have internal vs external models; external must live in a dedicated tenancy. can Dedicated ensure isolation across teams?
[03:55] Samir: Dedicated gives you an isolated GPU pool; you can also create per-route model pinning and access controls. RBAC and network isolation map to your tenancy controls.
[04:06] Priya: about audit logs and traceability — we need immutable audit trails for model changes and inference access by user. is that built-in?
[04:12] Alex: yes, audit logs, per-request metadata, and tracing hooks can be exported to your SIEM. retention and immutability are configurable as an add-on.
[04:22] Jordan: performance tuning — what levers do we have? batching, kv cache, quantization? how much impact do each have?
[04:29] Samir: batching reduces cost per token but increases latency; KV cache helps with prefix-heavy workloads hugely; quantization reduces mem and cost but may have slight quality impact. Redwood Optimize gives profiles and recommendations per route.
[04:43] Maya: what's the typical SLA for p95 and availability on Dedicated?
[04:46] Alex: for committed Dedicated capacity we can offer SLA targets in the contract—examples: 99.9% uptime and p95 latency targets depending on instance family and config. we'll tailor the SLA to the capacity and usage patterns.
[04:59] Priya: legal/process question — procurement timeline: we usually need 6-8 weeks for vendor onboarding, security review, and contract. we want to align pilot so it completes before procurement finish if possible.
[05:09] Alex: understood; we'll aim to start a pilot quickly while contracting runs.
[05:15] Maya: pilot scope — what do you recommend?
[05:18] Samir: a 2-week pilot: 1) deploy a small dedicated pool (1-2 GPUs) with your latency-sensitive routes, 2) run throughput and p95 tests (steady + burst), 3) run accuracy regression tests against your prompt set, 4) evaluate KV cache hit rates and batching efficiency.
[05:33] Jordan: helpful. we can provide a traffic trace and representative prompts.
[05:37] Priya: security docs — please send SOC2, pen test reports, and KMS architecture.
[05:41] Alex: will do. we'll share the security bundle and contract template after the call.
[05:46] Maya: any gotchas for cloud provider compatibility? we run primarily in AWS (us-east-1).
[05:51] Samir: full support for AWS Dedicated with VPC peering, and we can run customer-managed nodes if you need. minor differences in instance families across clouds, but we provide vendor guidance.
[06:01] Jordan: what about observability — do we get per-route token-level cost and latency dashboards?
[06:06] Alex: yes, Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost, per-model and per-route latency, traces, and error analysis. you'll get role-based access to those dashboards.
[06:15] Maya: decision criteria — what would push us to Hosted vs Dedicated?
[06:19] Alex: Hosted is fastest to run and cheaper for sporadic usage; Dedicated wins for isolation, predictable latency, and cost predictability at scale. also easier for compliance since you can restrict network and key access.
[06:32] Maya: ok, sounds like Dedicated with a pilot.
[06:35] Samir: next steps recap: we'll share pricing, security docs, and a benchmark plan. you provide traffic traces and prompt sets. then schedule pilot kickoff.
[06:44] Jordan: timeline — we want pilot in mid-March. procurement will take longer but pilot can run while contracts are negotiated.
[06:51] Priya: I want to review the contract for liability and data residency clauses early.
[06:55] Alex: understood — we'll flag those items in the contract and include data residency options.
[07:00] Maya: cool. any last technical clarifications?
[07:03] Samir: one small note on KV cache — large context and prefix reuse drives big wins; we'll instrument your traces to estimate hit rate.
[07:10] Jordan: sounds good. thanks all.
[07:13] Alex: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of transcript.

Note: Transcript contains occasional minor transcription errors, speaker overlaps, and shorthand (KM S -> KMS, etc.).
